author: reek
body: Codex source, classified into coloured runs. This is the half of syntax highlighting that has nothing to do with a screen: it takes one line of source and answers where each token starts, how long it is, and what kind of thing it is. Drawing is somebody else's job, which is what lets this be tested without a framebuffer.

author: reek
body: EVERY CHARACTER TEST GOES THROUGH THE CCE PREDICATES. Codex text is CCE internally, not ASCII: `a` is 15 and `e` is 13, digits are 3 to 12, and a space is 2. A classifier written against ASCII ranges answers that no line contains a letter, which is the bug `text-to-upper` shipped with for as long as it did. So `is-letter`, `is-digit`, `is-upper` and `is-whitespace` come from Foreword chapter CCE, and the three punctuation characters this file needs are derived from Text literals with `syn-ch` rather than written as numbers. A literal's characters are already CCE, so the derivation cannot drift the way a hardcoded 45 for a hyphen would.

author: reek
body: SynPlain is the honest answer for anything unrecognised, and it exists so that an unclassified character is drawn in the foreground colour rather than dropped. A highlighter that silently omits what it does not understand loses source off the screen.

author: reek
body: One letter per class, for tests and for reading a classification at a glance. The runtime path never calls this.

author: reek
body: The three characters this file must recognise by identity rather than by category, derived from literals so they are CCE by construction.

author: reek
body: `cites`, `quotes`, `grounds` and `trusting` are split out as directives rather than keywords because they are the chapter header's vocabulary and a reader looks for them as a block. `above` stays a keyword: it is only ever the tail of `trusting above N`, and colouring a bare `above` as a directive would be a lie in any other position.

author: reek
body: A word that begins with an upper-case letter is a type, which is the whole of Codex's naming convention: types are PascalCase and values are kebab-case, so the first character settles it with no table.

author: reek
body: A hyphen continues a name only when a letter or a digit follows it, which is exactly the compiler's rule and is what keeps `x - 1` a subtraction, `a-2` one identifier, and `a->b` an arrow rather than a name called `a-`.

author: reek
body: A string runs to its closing quote, and a backslash inside it consumes the character after it so an escaped quote does not end the run. An unterminated string ends at the end of the line rather than running off it: a half-typed line is the normal state of an editor buffer, and a classifier that faulted on one would be useless in the place it is most wanted.

author: reek
body: One tag character per source character, gaps included, so a test can compare a whole line's classification as a string. This is what makes the classifier falsifiable without a screen: the expected output names every character's class, so a token that grows, shrinks or changes kind moves the line.

author: reek
body: XRGB, and deliberately a fixed palette rather than a Theme lookup. The GOP text primitive takes a packed colour and nothing on that path carries a Theme; wiring one through to reach six constants would be an abstraction for a single implementation, which is the thing `VisionAndVirtues` virtue 7 says not to build. When a second consumer wants different colours, that is the moment for a parameter.
